title: Infra GPU Fleet, Capacity, IaC & CI/CD Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary

This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's operational guidance for managing the GPU fleet, capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD build pipelines, and related runbooks. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners who operate inference capacity for Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployments.

Scope

- Fleet sizing and burst-capacity strategy for inference GPU pools
- Terraform module usage patterns and versioning conventions
- CI/CD build and release flow for infra modules and runtime images
- Cloud account network design (VPCs, subnetting, peering, and egress controls)
- Runbook procedures for capacity incidents, scaling, and planned maintenance

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: Infra Engineering (infra-gpu@redwood.ai)
- Pager: Infra on-call (see oncall rota)
- Product / Serving Runtime liaison: Samira Khan (serving-runtime@redwood.ai)
- Capacity forecasting owner: Marcus Nguyen

Definitions and terminology

- GPU pool: logical group of nodes with identical sizing and model variants (e.g., gpus-nvidia-a100-80gb-prod)
- Reserved capacity: contractual pool for Dedicated customers (guaranteed T/second)
- Burst capacity: ephemeral spot-backed nodes for smoothing spikes
- KV-cache nodes: specialized instances that hold long-running KV cache state

Architecture overview

- Control plane (k8s, control-plane cluster) manages allocation and routing of requests to GPU pools.
- Serving runtime runs on GPU nodes orchestrated by Fleet Manager (service: infra-fleet-manager).
- Autoscaling controller (service: infra-autoscaler) adjusts capacity using metrics from Prometheus and the cost predictor service.
- IaC: Terraform modules live in git repo infra/terraform/modules, published with semantic versions and CI checks.

SLOs and operational thresholds

- P95 latency (generation): <= 250 ms for small models; <= 1200 ms for long-sequence generation (SLO depends on model class).
- Pool utilization target: 60-75% steady state (keeps headroom for bursts).
- Alert: Pool utilization > 80% sustained for 10 minutes -> P1 (scale-immediately)
- Alert: Failed allocation rate > 1% over 5m -> P1

Capacity planning model (summary)

- Inputs: current qps by route, token distribution, average tokens per request, model concurrency per GPU, pre-warm ratio, historical growth rate.
- Buffer policy: keep 20% headroom on top of 95th percentile demand for Hosted; 10% for Dedicated (contracted).

Capacity calculator (example table)

| Metric | Example value | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| 95th qps (tokens/sec) | 120k | across all regions for model family X |
| avg tokens / request | 120 | prompts + responses |
| tokens/sec per GPU | 8k | depends on model and quantization profile |
| required GPUs | 15 | ceil((120k / 8k) * 1.2 buffer) |

GPU pool types and recommended sizing

- a100-80gb (prod-large): best for high-memory LLMs and KV-cache nodes. Use when model requires >40GB RAM.
- a100-40gb (prod): cost-effective for many 70B models with quantization.
- h100 (experimental): used in benchmarks; enable only after perf sign-off.
- spot-burst pools: set taints/tolerations and max eviction tolerant workloads only.

Terraform / IaC modules

Principles
- Modules must be small and focused (networking, gpu-pool, iam-roles, autoscaler).
- All modules expose clear inputs/outputs and maintain major-minor patch releases.
- State strategy: per-account per-environment state buckets with locking (S3 + Dynamo or cloud-equivalent).

Example module usage (terraform)

module "gpu_pool_prod" {
  source = "github.com/redwood/infra-terraform//modules/gpu-pool?ref=v1.6.0"
  name   = "gpus-nvidia-a100-80gb-prod"
  region = "us-west-2"
  node_count = 16
  instance_type = "gpu.a100.80gb"
  resource_tags = { team = "infra" env = "prod" }
}

Module publishing/CI requirements
- Lint (tflint), fmt (terraform fmt) and unit tests (terratest) run on every PR.
- Release process: tag Vx.y.z -> build pipeline publishes changelog and updates module registry.
- Backwards compatibility: additions only; breaking changes must go through ADR and a major version bump.

CI/CD and build pipelines

Repository layout and pipeline responsibilities
- infra/terraform: module CI and plan/apply workflows. Plan runs on PRs, apply only after approvals and matched branch (release/*).
- infra/images: container builds for runtime images and test harnesses. Images are built via GitHub Actions with multi-arch caching and pushed to our ECR/GCR.
- infra/helm-charts: chart linting and snapshot release to internal Helm registry.

Sample pipeline steps (high level)
1. PR -> terraform fmt + tflint + unit tests
2. Terraform plan with var diff; post plan in PR comment
3. Manual approval from infra owners (2 approvers) -> apply on protected branch
4. Post-deploy smoke tests: run minimal inference load (smoke-suite) against new pool
5. Monitor metrics for 15 minutes; auto-rollback on failure conditions (see rollback section)

Example GitHub Actions snippet (conceptual)

name: terraform-apply
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  apply:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      - name: Terraform Init & Apply
        run: |
          terraform init -backend-config="bucket=${{ secrets.STATE_BUCKET }}"
          terraform apply -auto-approve

Network and cloud accounts

Account design
- Per-environment accounts: prod, staging, dev, ci (separate org units).
- Dedicated customer accounts are isolated VPCs with peered access to control-plane via Transit Gateway or VPC peering.

VPC & subnet guidance
- Use 3 AZs per region; create public and private subnets per AZ.
- NATs: centralized NAT gateway per AZ for predictable egress costs.
- Security groups: deny-all by default; explicitly open inference ports (8000-8010) and SSH only from bastion subnets.

Peering and routing
- Use Transit Gateway for multi-VPC routing in prod; avoid full mesh.
- Route tables: ensure return path to control plane and monitoring VPCs.
- Egress policies: route outbound model artifact download traffic through egress proxies to enforce allowlists and caching.

Key operational runbooks

1) High utilization / allocation failures (P1)
- Trigger: Alert "pool-utilization>80% (10m)" or "allocation-failed-rate>1%"
- Triage steps:
  1. Ack alert in PagerDuty and assign to on-call.
  2. Check infra-autoscaler logs and Prometheus metrics (query: sum by(pool) (gpu_utilization))
  3. If autoscaler is not scaling: inspect controller logs and reconcile with Terraform desired_count.
  4. Manual scale: terraform apply a temporary node_count increase (increase by +25%) and run smoke-suite.
  5. Notify customers via status page if Dedicated customers are affected.
  6. Post-incident: update demand forecast and adjust pre-warm policy.

2) Node eviction of spot-burst pool (P2/P3)
- Trigger: Spot termination notice or increased eviction rate.
- Steps:
  1. Drain evicted nodes: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data <node>
  2. Re-schedule critical workloads to reserved pool using node selectors/taints.
  3. If sustained, increase reserved pool capacity by +10% and reduce spot fraction.

3) Failed Terraform apply (sensitive infra change)
- Trigger: apply fails on protected branch
- Steps:
  1. Re-run plan locally with same backend and variables.
  2. Inspect state lock and S3/Dynamo entries.
  3. If state corruption suspected, restore from last known-good state snapshot, re-run plan.
  4. If changes are breaking, open an ADR and coordinate a scheduled rollout.

Rollout and rollback procedure

- Canary first: deploy new node pool to canary AZ or tag 5% of traffic using routing policies.
- Smoke tests: functional inference (latency, correctness) and load test at 5-10% traffic for 30 minutes.
- Roll forward: increase traffic by doubling canary every 30 minutes until 100%.
- Rollback: revert Terraform module to previous module version and apply. Automated rollback triggers: error-rate>2% or p95 latency degradation > 1.5x baseline for 15 minutes.

Maintenance windows and scheduled work

- Weekly maintenance window: Tue 02:00-04:00 UTC for non-prod; monthly windows for prod with 72-hour notice.
- For Dedicated customers: coordinate maintenance with account owners and provide maintenance plans 7 days in advance.

Observability and dashboards

- Dashboards: Pool-level dashboard (utilization, p95 latency, allocation success rate).
- Alerts: configured in Prometheus Alertmanager and routed via PagerDuty with runbooks linked.
- Logs: infra-fleet-manager and infra-autoscaler logs stored in centralized logging (ELK/CloudWatch) with 90-day retention.

Security & access controls

- IAM: least-privilege roles for Terraform pipelines and service accounts.
- Secrets: use KMS + secrets manager for image pull creds, cloud provider keys, and artifact storage.
- Network controls: private subnets for GPU pools; no public IPs on nodes.

Appendix: Terraform parameters (quick reference)

| Input | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| name | string | n/a | resource name for pool |
| region | string | us-west-2 | cloud region |
| node_count | number | 4 | initial desired nodes |
| instance_type | string | gpu.a100.80gb | instance flavor |
| pre_warm_ratio | number | 0.2 | fraction of extra nodes to keep warm |

End of playbook
